strengths: Addresses a well-scoped and practically important problem — real-time, streaming, infinite-length audio-driven avatar generation with a 14B diffusion backbone — and is transparent about the hardware requirement (20 FPS end-to-end with 4 NFE on 5xH800). The declared type is Algorithms/General, but the work is best read as an Applied/Systems contribution; judged as such, the demonstrated end-to-end system is substantial.

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) is a genuinely novel and generalizable inference paradigm: assigning each device a fixed timestep and pipelining the denoising chain converts a sequential diffusion bottleneck into a spatial pipeline. Reusing local, noise-aligned KV caches eliminates inter-GPU KV traffic while keeping communication to latents only, and the design is well supported (Table 3, Table 6, Fig. 8 timeline showing high DiT utilization).

The Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (Adaptive Attention Sink + Rolling RoPE) is a sensible and well-ablated remedy for long-horizon identity drift and color artifacts. Table 4 shows clear degradation when AAS, Rolling RoPE, or History Corrupt are removed, and the analysis of why inference-mode and distribution drift occur is convincing.

The empirical finding that noise-aligned ('timestep-forcing') KV caches outperform clean KV caches in both efficiency and perceptual quality (Table 6) is non-obvious and useful for the broader streaming-diffusion community; it also aligns the training-time noise state with inference-time behavior via History Corrupt.

Evidence for long-horizon stability is strong: a 10,000-second autoregressive rollout with nearly flat ASE/IQA/Sync-C/DINO-S between the 0-10 s and 10,000-10,010 s segments (Table 7, Fig. 9), far beyond the horizons reported by prior streaming video/avatar work.

Evaluation is broad: a custom OOD benchmark (GenBench-Short/Long), in-domain AVSpeech with FID/FVD, ablations of TPP, DMD, VAE parallelization, and RSFM components, plus a 20-participant double-blind user study. The paper is also candid that Sync-C/Sync-D can be gamed by exaggerated lip motion, motivating the perceptual study.

Clarity is generally good: informative figures, complete algorithm boxes for training and single-/multi-GPU inference in the supplement, and an explicit limitations and ethical-consideration discussion.
High impact potential for industrial long-form avatar synthesis; the paper convincingly bridges high-fidelity large-model generation and real-time streaming, a tension that has remained unresolved.
weaknesses: The efficiency claims are hardware-asymmetric and the 'real-time' framing is partly a multi-GPU artifact: 20.88 FPS requires 5 H800s, while Ditto and EchoMimic-V2 are run on a single GPU (per the supplement), and FPS is never normalized per GPU. Ditto, a 0.2B model, already reaches 21.8 FPS, so the honest differentiator is quality at 14B scale, not raw interactivity. In addition, TTFF of ~2.89 s is far from conversational latency and is only briefly acknowledged.

No quality ablation isolates the cost of TPP. Table 3 reports only speed for 'w/o TPP' / 'w/o TPP w/ SP_4GPU', so it is unclear whether the pipelined, noise-aligned-KV approximation degrades visual quality relative to exact sequential denoising. Table 6 conflates this with the separate question of KV-cache noise level.

Some claims are overstated or factually loose. On GenBench-ShortVideo the text states synchronization is 'better than ... StableAvatar', yet StableAvatar's Sync-C (6.77) exceeds ours (5.69) (Sync-D is mixed), and on AVSpeech our Sync-C (4.64) is clearly below OmniAvatar (6.04) and StableAvatar (5.72). The narrative underplays this lip-sync regression relative to baselines.

Table 1 lists InfiniteTalk as satisfying streaming, real-time, and infinite-length generation, yet InfiniteTalk never appears in any quantitative comparison (Tables 2 or 8). Since it is arguably the closest competitor on the infinite-length axis, this omission weakens the contextualization of the 'first' claim, which is otherwise only supported at 14B scale.

Attribution of quality gains to the proposed mechanisms is incomplete: the only within-family control is WanS2V, so part of the ASE/IQA advantage plausibly stems from backbone scale and DMD-based distillation rather than TPP/RSFM. A long-horizon comparison against a plain rolling-KV baseline (without RSFM) beyond the internal variants would strengthen the causal story.

Component novelty is partly incremental. Self-Forcing DMD, rolling KV caches, and sink-frame conditioning are established; RSFM is a combination of Adaptive Attention Sink and RoPE re-indexing. TPP is the strongest novel element, and the paper would benefit from stating more sharply what is new versus adapted.

Reproducibility is limited: training uses 128 H800 GPUs and ~500 GPU-days, no code/model release is mentioned (only a project page), and the OOD benchmark is synthetically generated with Gemini-2.5 Pro / Qwen-Image / CosyVoice without validation against real-world distributions — the reference frames and TTS audio may carry their own artifacts that interact with the reported metrics.

Minor presentation issues: notation inconsistencies (block index i vs t; Eq. 5 vs surrounding text in Sec. 4.1, where the KV-cache/noisy-block sentence is garbled), and the relationship between block-wise gradient accumulation and DMD's online update is only sketched in the supplement, slightly hindering understanding of the training procedure.

strengths: Targets a genuinely important and hard problem — real-time, streaming, arbitrarily long audio-driven avatar generation — and tackles it with an algorithm-system co-design at 14B scale, which is a non-trivial engineering undertaking (128 H800 training GPUs, 5-GPU streaming deployment).

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) is a clean, well-motivated idea: pinning each GPU to a fixed denoising timestep, keeping KV caches local (no inter-GPU KV communication), and offloading VAE decoding to a dedicated device. Figure 3 and the runtime timeline in Figure 8 make the mechanism and its utilization concrete.

The empirical study is broad by current standards: comparisons against six open-source baselines, an OOD synthetic benchmark, an in-domain AVSpeech hold-out (Table 8), component-wise ablations (Tables 3, 4, 6), a 10,000-second stress test, and a double-blind user study with 20 participants.

Ablations are informative and mostly well-chosen: the noisy-KV (timestep-forcing) vs. clean-KV study in Table 6 gives a plausible and useful empirical justification for a design choice that prior streaming systems have made differently.

The paper is generally well organized, the framework figure (Fig. 2) and the inference-settings diagrams (Figs. 6, 7) are instructive, and full pseudocode for training and both single-/multi-GPU inference is provided in the supplementary.
A limitations paragraph and an ethics discussion are present, and the 10,000 s rollout is a stronger long-horizon test than the ~4-minute horizons reported by prior work.
weaknesses: The core mechanism is under-specified in the main text. RSFM is defined by Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE, and History Corrupt, but all three are explicitly deferred to the supplementary material ("Details of AAS and Rolling RoPE are provided in the supplementary materials", footnote for History Corrupt). Section 4.4 is a qualitative narrative; a reader of the main paper cannot verify correctness or reimplement the components on which the headline long-horizon claims rest.

The efficiency claim is not compute-normalized and is partly contradicted by the paper's own numbers. Ours = 20.88 FPS using 5 H800 GPUs (Table 3), whereas Ditto is reported at 21.80 FPS on a single H800 (Table 2, Sec. 10). Thus the proposed system is not faster than an existing real-time method and costs roughly 5x the hardware; the abstract's "real-time … on 5 H800 GPUs" framing and the "breaking the autoregressive bottleneck" language oversell what is essentially (approximately) linear scaling in GPU count. No fixed-GPU-budget comparison against any baseline is reported.

TPP's scalability is fundamentally capped by the number of denoising steps (4 NFE here), so at most ~4–5 devices can be exploited; this ceiling is never discussed, and the method would not extend to higher-quality many-step samplers without using dozens of GPUs.

The most directly comparable prior art is cited but not compared. TalkingMachines [27], LLIA [51], ARIG [16], Teller [53], Midas [4] and StreamDiT [21] are all streaming/real-time avatar or interactive video methods; omitting them leaves the "state-of-the-art" and "first to achieve practical, real-time, high-fidelity avatar generation at this scale" claims unsupported. Table 1's streaming/real-time/infinite-length classification is also asserted rather than measured (e.g., Ditto is marked real-time ✓, OmniAvatar ✗, with no supporting protocol).

Results on standard metrics are mixed and in places contradict the claims. On GenBench-ShortVideo the method trails OmniAvatar substantially in lip-sync (Sync-C 5.69 vs. 6.77; Sync-D 9.13 vs. 7.59). On in-domain AVSpeech (Table 8) FID is 64.00 vs. Ditto's 46.27 and Sync-C is 4.64 vs. OmniAvatar's 6.04, i.e., the method does not dominate even in its training domain, yet it is described as "competitive or superior … across most metrics". The dismissal of Sync-C via THEval is applied asymmetrically — it is invoked when the method loses and ignored when it wins.

GenBench is entirely synthetic, generated by Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen-Image and CosyVoice, has no ground truth (so FID/FVD are unavailable), and is not validated as representative or as free of bias toward the proposed pipeline. The main long-video comparisons rest heavily on this unvalidated benchmark.

The "infinite-length" evidence is thin: Table 7 reports only four sampled windows of a single 10,000 s rollout with repeated ~10-minute audio, and the metrics are almost identical (ASE 3.37/3.38/3.37/3.38), which is either an under-informative measurement or a suspiciously flat one. No drift, identity-variation, or per-segment variance analysis is given, and repeating a short audio does not test true open-ended generation.

Component novelty is incremental and the delta over cited work is not clearly delineated. Self-Forcing DMD with noisy KV cache (History Corrupt) is a modification of Self-Forcing [19]; AAS and Rolling RoPE are variants of attention-sink and RoPE-shift tricks; and pipeline-parallel diffusion inference is an established family (PipeFusion/AsyncDiff/xDiT-style methods) that is neither discussed nor compared. The paper does not state crisply which parts are new versus recombined.

Reproducibility is weak: training requires ~500 GPU-days on 128 H800s, no code/model release is indicated, and several critical settings (block size and local attention window semantics, the History Corrupt noise schedule, how the sink frame is handled for arbitrary reference images, LoRA target modules) are only partially specified in the main text or relegated to footnotes.

The paper's own limitation admits that TPP "enhances FPS but does not reduce TTFF" (Table 3: 2.89 s end-to-end time-to-first-frame). For an interactive avatar system this is a substantial caveat that sits awkwardly with the "real-time streaming" and "interactive digital communication" framing in the abstract and introduction.

Presentation issues: Table 1 renders the method as "Live avatar(ours)" inconsistently with the rest of the paper; notation such as B^i_{t-1} = v_θ(B^i_t, B^{i-(i-w):(i-1)}, I, a^i, t^i) is not adequately explained in the main text; and multiple core details are only reachable through supplementary footnotes, which weakens the main paper as a standalone contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a substantial algorithm-system co-design contribution: Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) converts the sequential diffusion denoising chain into a distributed pipeline and achieves real-time streaming at 20.88 FPS with a 14B model on 5 H800 GPUs, which is a meaningful systems advance for large-scale audio-driven avatar generation.

The long-horizon consistency mechanism (Rolling Sink Frame / Adaptive Attention Sink / Rolling RoPE / History Corrupt) is well motivated, and the 10,000-second stress test plus long-video comparisons show strong stability in identity, color, and perceptual quality where several baselines visibly degrade.

The paper includes useful ablations: TPP, VAE parallelization, and DMD are clearly shown to be critical for real-time performance, and the long-video ablation supports the proposed rolling-sink components. Supplementary material adds pseudocode, implementation details, and AVSpeech in-domain results.

The problem is practically important, and the paper convincingly demonstrates that large diffusion models can be deployed under streaming, infinite-length, real-time constraints, even if the individual components build on prior work. The user study also partially addresses known weaknesses of automatic sync metrics.
The writing is generally clear at the high level, with a well-structured presentation of challenges, methods, experiments, limitations, and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: Novelty is mostly integrative: the method heavily relies on existing foundations such as Wan-S2V, Self-Forcing, CausVid, LongLive, DMD, and attention-sink/rolling-KV ideas. TPP and RSFM are useful engineering contributions, but the paper does not fully isolate which parts are fundamentally new versus careful system integration.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance is overstated for short-video benchmarks: in Table 2, the method is not best on ASE, IQA, or Sync-C, and it only clearly wins on long-video quality and speed. The speed comparison is also not fully apples-to-apples, since Ditto achieves similar/slightly higher FPS with a 0.2B model, while this work uses 5 H800 GPUs and a 14B model.

Reproducibility is limited: no code/model release is stated, training requires 128 H800 GPUs and about 500 GPU days, and key implementation details such as the exact History Corrupt noise schedule/magnitude are not sufficiently specified or ablated. The GenBench benchmark is synthetically generated and apparently not released, raising concerns about evaluation generality.

Several technical details are underspecified or inconsistent. Equation 5 uses confusing notation for blocks, timesteps, and KV caches; the pseudocode in Algorithms 1-2 has ambiguous indexing; Algorithm 4 appears to broadcast a decoded sink frame rather than the VAE-encoded sink latent expected by the model. These issues hinder a precise understanding and reproduction of TPP/AAS/Rolling RoPE.

The empirical evaluation lacks statistical rigor in places: the user study has only 20 participants and no confidence intervals or significance tests, and long-video results are averaged over a small number of synthetic videos without variance reporting. The ablation table captions and row descriptions are also ambiguous, e.g., it is unclear exactly which components are removed in the 'w/o AAS' and 'w/o History Corrupt' settings.

Limitations are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed: TPP does not reduce TTFF, and its scalability is questionable when denoising steps exceed available GPUs or when more complex sampling schedules are needed. The strong dependence on RSFM and the use of noisy KV caches are interesting but not theoretically justified.

strengths: Presents Live Avatar, a substantial algorithm-system co-design that, to my knowledge, is the first practical real-time streaming framework for a 14B diffusion model for audio-driven avatar generation, with strong empirical speed and long-horizon results.

The two-stage distillation pipeline is well motivated and supported: Stage 1 diffusion forcing pretraining with motion-frame scaffolding, Stage 2 Self-Forcing DMD with History Corrupt, and a reported 5x Stage-2 convergence speedup with ablation evidence.

Long-horizon stability is convincingly addressed through complementary strategies: History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, and Rolling RoPE; ablations and 10,000-second extrapolation results show stable metrics and visual fidelity across long rollouts.

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) is a creative systems contribution that reparameterizes sequential diffusion sampling into an asynchronous spatial pipeline, enabling 45.2 FPS and 1.21s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs with minimal inter-GPU communication.

The empirical study is extensive and largely transparent: comparisons to state-of-the-art methods on GenBench and AVSpeech, short/long benchmark splits, efficiency ablations, visual ablations, user study, appendix pseudo-code, and detailed runtime metrics.
The paper is clearly written, and the supplementary material provides extensive implementation, algorithmic, and evaluation details that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Several components are adapted from existing work (Self-Forcing, DMD, Diffusion Forcing, RoPE, attention sink, WanS2V backbone), so the primary novelty lies in integration and system-level co-design rather than a fundamentally new generative paradigm.

The real-time claim should be qualified: TTFF is 1.21s on 5 H800 GPUs, but the paper acknowledges approximately 3s end-to-end latency with network transport, which does not yet meet the stringent requirements of bidirectional real-time interaction.

The 'infinite-length' claim is demonstrated only up to 10,000 seconds in the supplementary material; while impressive, this is a finite stress test and not a proof of truly infinite stable generation.

GenBench is synthetically generated using Gemini-2.5 Pro, Qwen-Image, and CosyVoice, and the long subset contains only 15 videos; this may not fully represent real-world avatar distributions, and ground-truth-free metrics can be exploited by models with exaggerated motion.

The efficiency comparison may not fully normalize hardware and parallelism: the proposed method uses TPP over multiple GPUs while some baselines use fewer GPUs or smaller models, so wall-clock FPS comparisons should be interpreted with care.

Some design choices, such as using noisy KV cache as a low-pass filter and timestep-forcing for flicker reduction, are supported mainly by empirical results and intuitive arguments rather than deeper theoretical analysis.

Reproducibility is partially deferred: GenBench and evaluation scripts are promised for the camera-ready version, and access to the pretrained WanS2V model, AVSpeech data, and the synthetic generative models may impose licensing or availability constraints for independent verification.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: real-time streaming audio-driven avatar generation with long-horizon stability, combining algorithmic and systems contributions.

The system-level contribution is substantial: Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) distributes denoising steps across GPUs, enabling 45 FPS and 1.21s TTFF for a 14B diffusion model on 5 H800 GPUs, with useful engineering details in the supplement.

Extensive experiments and ablations are provided, including GenBench short/long video comparisons, AVSpeech in-domain evaluation, long-horizon stress tests to 10,000 seconds, and ablations for History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE, denoising step count, KV-cache noise scheduling, and block size.

The long-horizon stabilization strategies (History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE) are well motivated and target distinct failure modes: error accumulation, distribution drift, and test-time conditioning drift.
The paper is generally clearly organized, with supplementary pseudo-code, algorithmic visualizations, inference timelines, and ethical consideration.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern: no code, model weights, benchmark data, or evaluation scripts are provided in the submission; GenBench and scripts are only promised for the camera-ready version, and training/inference relies on 128 H800 GPUs plus proprietary or large pretrained components, making independent verification difficult.

The GenBench benchmark contribution is not yet validated: it is synthesized with proprietary models (Gemini-2.5 Pro, Qwen-Image, CosyVoice) without human verification, has only 100 short clips and 15 long videos, and lacks ground-truth references for long-video evaluation, so the claim of a standardized long-form benchmark is currently unsupported.

The 'real-time' and 'infinite-length' claims are overstated: TTFF of 1.21s plus network transport yields ~3s end-to-end latency, which does not meet real-time interactive requirements, and the paper only demonstrates 10,000 seconds (under 3 hours), not infinite generation, with no theoretical guarantee.

Methodological novelty is limited relative to existing work: TPP is an intuitive pipeline-parallel extension of diffusion denoising, while the long-horizon strategies build heavily on Self-Forcing, DMD, noisy KV caches, and attention sinks. Related pipeline-parallel diffusion methods and recent streaming-video baselines (e.g., PipeFusion/DistriFusion, LongLive, Self-Forcing++) are not adequately compared or discussed.

Evaluation fairness is questionable: the proposed method is heavily optimized with kernel-level FP8 quantization, FlashAttention, graph compilation, LoRA merging, and 5-GPU inference, while some baselines run on a single GPU or at different resolutions, so speed comparisons are not apples-to-apples. Several baseline numbers may also be stale or self-reimplemented.

The user study uses only 20 participants without statistical significance testing, and it shows WanS2V achieves higher Naturalness than the proposed method, yet the paper still emphasizes broad superiority; perceptual metrics such as Q-Align and Sync-C/D can be gamed and do not fully capture naturalness or real-world quality.

Technical details in the main paper are incomplete: AAS and Rolling RoPE are relegated to the supplementary, motion-frame scaffold details are ambiguous, and dataset preprocessing/training specifics are sparse, which hampers scientific assessment.

The paper overclaims practical impact: reliance on 5 H800 GPUs for streaming, lack of released code/benchmark, and the admitted latency limitation undercut the 'practical real-time' framing, despite the otherwise interesting system design.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: real-time, streaming, infinite-length audio-driven avatar generation with a large 14B diffusion model, with clear application value for interactive digital humans.

Presents a coherent algorithm-system co-design: the two-stage causal distillation with motion-frame scaffold, long-horizon stability strategies (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE), and Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) are each motivated and empirically ablated.

Reports strong empirical results: 45.2 FPS and 1.21s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs, stable generation to 10,000 seconds, and competitive/superior performance on GenBench short/long and AVSpeech against several state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics.
Introduces GenBench (Short/Long), a benchmark for long-form audio-driven avatar generation, addressing a gap in standardized long-duration evaluation; dataset and scripts are promised.

Provides extensive experiments and ablation studies covering inference efficiency, long-horizon stability strategies, denoising step count, KV-cache noise scheduling, block size, FP8 quantization, user study, and 10,000-second extrapolation.
Clear exposition and detailed supplementary material: pseudocode, training/inference details, kernel-level optimizations, and qualitative analyses facilitate understanding and future work.
Acknowledges limitations including static-scene prior, compute requirements, and end-to-end latency, which helps contextualize the claims.
weaknesses: Practicality is limited by hardware: real-time streaming requires 5 high-end H800 GPUs and training uses 128 H800 GPUs, making the system inaccessible to most labs and weakening the 'practical real-time' claim.
End-to-end interaction latency is approximately 3 seconds, as the authors acknowledge; TTFF plus network transport does not yet meet the stringent requirements of bidirectional real-time interaction.

Infinite-length stability relies on a static-scene/avatar prior and is demonstrated mainly on 15 synthetic long videos; generalization to dynamic backgrounds, large pose changes, or scene transitions is not established.

Algorithmic novelty is partly incremental: the method builds heavily on Self-Forcing and DMD, while the main novel technical contribution is TPP plus specific long-horizon fixes; a stronger comparison against concurrent streaming diffusion systems would help.

Comparisons are incomplete: InfiniteTalk appears in Table 1 but is absent from quantitative experiments; EchoMimic-V2 is excluded from long-video comparison, and the long GenBench set is small and synthetic.

Evaluation metrics have known limitations: Sync-C/Sync-D can be gamed by exaggerated motion, and the user study (20 participants) partially mitigates but does not fully resolve this; FID/FVD are only reported in-domain.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: GenBench and evaluation scripts are promised for camera-ready, but full model/training/inference code is not clearly released, and the large training compute makes independent reproduction difficult.
The abstract contains an incomplete 'Our project page is at .' statement, which should be fixed; minor presentation issues remain despite otherwise clear writing.
